question: In 1985 the EEC submitted a démarche highlighting the illegality of the “Libyan Claim over the Gulf of Sidra, violating the applicable international customary law”. In December 2005, the European Council protested to Libya following Libya’s approval in June 2005 of Resolution 104 on straight baselines for Libyan territorial waters and Resolution 105 defining a Libyan protected fishing zone.

The Council stressed that the Libyan baselines were not marked out in accordance with the provisions of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea relating to demarcation lines for marine gulfs. Furthermore, the European Council’s resolutions on Libya, 2018/2017(INI) and 2021/2064(INI), expressly refer to protection of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

To ‘close’ a gulf which is considered to be ‘internal waters’, the maximum distance should be 24 nautical miles. In the case of the Gulf of Sidra, the opening is more than 180 nautical miles wide. The unlawful government of Libya refers to historical rights in its attempt to claim the entire Gulf of Sidra.
I ask the Vice-President of the Commission/High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy: 1.
What steps will he take to ensure that any initiative by Libya that contravenes the provisions of UNCLOS will be annulled in practice?
How does he intend to ensure that Libya does not commit similar unlawful acts in the future?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.4.2024) Under international law, the establishment of baselines and maritime zones under sovereignty or national jurisdiction is a competence that belongs to States.

The EU firmly believes that maritime delimitation disputes need to be settled by peaceful means, notably through negotiations, and in full respect of international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). With regard to the issue of Libyan maritime demarcation lines, the European Council of December 20191 clearly set out its position, which remains unchanged2.

This position was reiterated in October 20223, following the signing of a new Memorandum of Understanding between Türkiye and the Libyan Government of National Unity. The EU holds the view that the 2019 Turkey-Libya Memorandum of Understanding4 infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states, does not comply with the Law of the Sea and cannot produce any legal consequences for third states.
